title: Banks told 'stick to your lane' over loan refusals
full_text:
The Coalition says it will try to stop banks imposing bans on loans to otherwise credit-worthy businesses requesting finance for coal, gas and forestry projects.
Assistant shadow treasurer Kevin Hogan said he would introduce a private members' bill into parliament to stop Australia's major banks using "ideological" policies that "debank" lawful industries.
He said banks should focus on whether a business can repay a loan, not whether it aligns with their political agenda.
"Big banks should stick to banking. That's what they're good at. They don't need to be activists - we have enough of them already," Hogan said.
"Banks have every right to reject a bad credit loan. But they shouldn't have policies that blacklist entire lawful industries because they don't like what they do."
The push is largely symbolic at this stage as the proposed law will not be supported by Labor and the Greens. The Coalition would need to win an election to have any hope of legislating the crackdown on the environmental, social and governance policies of banks.
But the policy deepens divisions between the Coalition and big banks, after former opposition leader Peter Dutton last year attacked "woke" bankers for rejecting loans on environmental grounds.
Separately, Coalition energy spokesman Dan Tehan last month vowed to scrap emissions rules for vehicles and industry, abandon four offshore wind zones and repeal the Climate Change Act to remove net zero targets.
The big banks declined to comment and deferred to the industry lobby group for a response.
Australian Banking Association chief executive Simon Birmingham said Hogan's plan was more regulation.
"This proposal for yet more red tape is completely unnecessary as Australian banks continue to finance businesses right across the economy, including in all parts of the energy sector," he said.
"Ideology or politics is in no way involved in providing finance with banks making lending decisions based on risk and balancing their legal and regulatory obligations."
The big banks have made various ESG commitments that prevent or make it harder to lend for fossil fuel projects and other industries such as forestry. However, banks have wound back applying some of those rules, following US President Donald Trump's retreat from climate change action and global financial institutions falling into line.
The Coalition's proposed law would stop industry blacklists, force banks to explain their decisions to customers, give businesses 90 days before an existing credit facility was unwound and give small businesses a right of review.
The rule would not apply to smaller customer-owned and specialist banks.
Hogan met the big four bank chief executives to discuss the ESG issues in the months leading up to the announcement on Tuesday.
He said banks would still be able to reject loans based on repayment capacity, security, legal requirements and genuine financial risks.
"This isn't about forcing banks to make bad loans. It's about stopping them from making political decisions," he said.
